summary: Gives an overview of the High-level Entity Management System (HEMS), an experimental system for managing hosts, gateways and other network entities. It was being tested in parts of the Internet at the time. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: The High-Level Entity Management System (HEMS) describes a shared way for programs to monitor and control network devices. Its design uses queries, event messages and applications, with more attention to monitoring than control.

questions: how was network management done before snmp
what is the high-level entity management protocol

subtitle: An overview of an experimental system for managing IP network entities.

tldr.problem: More vendors and growing networks made it difficult to manage network equipment through separate vendor-specific tools.
tldr.mechanism: HEMS combines query processors on managed entities, event generators and management applications that communicate using HEMP.
tldr.outcome: The memo describes an experimental system intended to help lead to a standard for IP network management; this RFC is Historic.

today: RFC 1021 is Historic. It described an experimental system, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why HEMS Was Proposed
sections.content:
The memo says that a growing number of vendors and interconnected IP networks made management difficult. Vendors had different management protocols, and no accepted standard covered network components. HEMS was an experimental effort intended to help develop a standard for IP internetwork management.

The memo distinguishes monitoring, which collects information about network behavior, from control, which changes that behavior. The authors focused more on monitoring because control is harder to define across diverse devices; strong access-control mechanisms were among the control components not fully defined.
sections.plainLanguage: Different vendors used different ways to manage their equipment, making a growing network harder to oversee. HEMS proposed shared monitoring and control methods, but focused first on monitoring.

sections.title: The Parts of HEMS
sections.content:
HEMS has three parts: a query processor on a managed entity, an event generator on entities, and applications that send requests and interpret replies. The query processor handles monitoring and control requests and works with self-describing objects encoded using a limited subset of ASN.1. A request can contain multiple instructions.

Each entity must manage a small standard set of objects. Some entity types may have additional required objects, and entities may expose their own objects. Events are unsolicited status messages, handled as specialized replies and sent to one or more management centers.
sections.plainLanguage: A management application asks a device's query processor for information or a change. The device can also send an event when it has status information to report.

sections.title: Messages and Transport Choices
sections.content:
Applications and query processors communicate with the High-Level Entity Management Protocol (HEMP), which formats queries and replies. HEMP runs over a transport protocol. The memo separates occasional status monitoring, troubleshooting a failing network, and event reporting because they have different reliability needs.

For troubleshooting, the memo says reliable delivery is essential for diagnostic information and control requests. Events need not be delivered reliably and may go to several management centers. The proposed transport choices are VMTP for more experimental systems, or TCP and UDP together for near-term production systems, as described in RFC 1022.
sections.plainLanguage: HEMP formats requests and replies, while another protocol carries them. The memo recommends reliable delivery for troubleshooting but allows event messages to use an unreliable transport.

sections.title: Compatibility With CMIP
sections.content: The memo says applications that use both HEMS and the emerging Common Management Information Protocol (CMIP) are feasible. Both systems operate on objects stored in remote entities and use ASN.1 to represent those objects. The memo suggests that shared interface routines could access either system even though their underlying mechanics differ.
sections.plainLanguage: HEMS and CMIP work differently internally, but both represent remote objects with ASN.1. The memo says this makes common access routines possible.

items.title: Query processor
items.text: Handles monitoring and control requests on an entity.

items.title: Event generator
items.text: Sends unsolicited status messages to management centers.
